summary: This informational document describes web-based real-time communication use cases and derives requirements on browser functionality from them. It was written in an early phase of the work and has not been revised much since, so it should be read as background.

plainLanguage.summary: This document lists what people want to do with live sound and video in a web browser, then turns each activity into a numbered demand on the browser. It records early thinking from the WebRTC working group, not a final set of rules.

subtitle: What web browsers need to support real-time voice, video, and data communication

tldr.problem: Web applications wanted to offer video calls, screen sharing and voice chat inside a browser, but nobody had written down what a browser has to be able to do for that to work.
tldr.mechanism: The document describes a set of use cases, from a one-to-one call to a group call and a game with voice, and derives numbered requirements on the browser from each one.
tldr.outcome: It was published in an early phase of the work to record the working group's conclusions rather than to set rules, and it is not a standard that later specifications or implementations are held to.

facts.label: Use case groups
facts.value: Browser-to-browser, and browser to gateway or server

today: RFC 7478 is an Informational document with no obsoleting or updating RFC recorded against it, so it remains the record of the working group's early conclusions rather than a current standard. The document itself says it was published for that purpose and will not be used as a rigid set of guidelines that specifications and implementations are held to.

sections.title: What the Document Sets Out to Do
sections.content:
RFC 7478 is an informational document that lists scenarios where a web application running in a browser exchanges live sound, video and data in real time, and turns each scenario into a numbered requirement on the browser. The scenarios range from a one-to-one video call between two browsers to a group call with no central server, an online game with voice chat, and a call that reaches an ordinary telephone network.

The browser requirements are numbered F1 to F36 and are listed next to the use case that produced them. A second set, numbered A1 to A26, covers the programming interface the web application uses; these sit in Appendix A and are not normative, because the W3C WebRTC working group is responsible for the API and decided to use this document's use cases and requirements instead of writing its own.

The authors are explicit about the document's standing. It was written in an initial phase of the work, with rather minor updates at later stages. It is published to record the early conclusions of the working group, and it will not be used as a set of rigid guidelines that specifications and implementations are held to in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: This document lists what people want to do with live sound and video in a browser, then turns each activity into a numbered demand on the browser. The authors say it records early conclusions, not rules that later work must follow.

sections.title: Use Cases and the Networks They Run On
sections.content:
The base scenario, the simple video communication service, has two users load the same web application, log in, and select each other as online. The service pushes login status to the application in each browser, and a one-to-one audiovisual session starts between the two browsers. The invited user may accept or reject. While the session is being set up the user sees a self view; afterwards the remote video is shown alongside it.

The document lists network conditions that apply to every use case: a client may be on an IPv4-only network, an IPv6-only network, or a dual-stack one; it may be on a link with a different throughput from its peer, on a variable-quality wireless link, or on a congested link; it may sit behind a firewall that allows no UDP; and it may sit behind a NAT or an IPv4-IPv6 translation device with any of the mapping and filtering behaviours described in RFC 4787.

Most of the other browser-to-browser use cases start from the simple video communication service and add one demand. A firewall that blocks UDP adds F18. A firewall that only permits traffic through an HTTP proxy adds F21. A service provider spread over a large area wants several STUN and TURN servers for IPv4 and IPv6 support, load balancing and redundancy, which adds F19; an enterprise that wants to audit sessions from inside its network supplies its own STUN and TURN servers, which adds F20. A user who moves from Ethernet to Wi-Fi to cellular mid-call adds F17, which requires the session to survive a change of network interface. Screen sharing adds F36 and file exchange adds F35.

Two use cases scale the model up. Multiparty video communication has no central server: each participant's browser sends and receives streams to and from all the others, renders several streams at once, mixes the audio locally, places each speaker in a different position in the room, and measures and adjusts the voice activity level. Multiparty online game with voice communication keeps the voice part and adds sound objects from another source, such as a file with the sound of a moving tank, mixed into the spatialised audio; quick game state updates are needed and have a higher priority than the voice, which adds F34 for short-latency unreliable datagram traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes a basic video call and then adds one new demand for each problem that can appear: a firewall that blocks UDP, a proxy-only firewall, a large service provider, a corporate network that wants to audit calls, a user who changes network mid-call, screen sharing and file transfer. It also covers group calls with no central server and voice chat inside an online game.

sections.title: Calls That Reach a Gateway or a Central Server
sections.content:
Not every client in these scenarios is a browser. A mobile telephony operator can let its customers make and receive calls from a browser that behaves like a normal phone, showing the caller's identity and the call history. The browser must support an audio codec that existing telephony services already understand (F31) and must be able to start and accept a media session whose setup data can be carried in SIP (F33).

In the FedEx call scenario a user dials a public telephone number from the browser, hears the prompts of an interactive voice response system and needs a way to navigate it when it says to press 1. The browser must support a dual-tone multi-frequency (DTMF) based interactive voice response system, which is requirement F32.

The third scenario puts a central conference server in the middle. Each participant's browser sends an audio stream to the server; the server mixes the streams, adding effects such as spatialisation if it likes, and returns one mixed stream to each participant. Video goes the same way, but the server shows one participant at full resolution in a large window and the others as small thumbnails, choosing which streams to forward based on speech activity. Because the choice changes often as the conversation moves, the delay from selecting a stream to displaying it has to be short. The document lists three ways to achieve this: a browser sends one high-resolution scalable stream and the server sends only its base layer for thumbnails; the browser sends one high and one low resolution stream in a simulcast fashion and the server selects; or the browser sends one high-resolution stream and the server transcodes it. The requirement added here is F16, which asks the browser to insert reference frames into an outgoing stream when the peer requests them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some calls do not go straight from browser to browser. The document covers calls into the ordinary telephone network, calls where the user must press keys to navigate an automated phone menu, and group calls that run through a central server. In the last case the server mixes everyone's voices and picks whose face to show large, so the browser has to react quickly when that choice changes.

sections.title: The Requirement List
sections.content:
Section 3 collects the browser requirements and groups them. The common and basic group runs from F1, which asks the browser to use microphones and cameras as input devices, to F15, which asks it to collect statistics about the transport of audio and video between peers so that quality of experience can be estimated. Between them sit the demands to send streams and data in the presence of NATs (F2), to rate control transmitted streams and data so the send rate drops when there is congestion (F3), to receive, process and render what peers send (F4), to keep good quality under reasonable jitter and packet loss (F5), to detect when a peer's stream stops arriving (F6), to make echo cancellation available when sound is both sent and received (F7), to synchronise audio and video (F8), to encode for the current rendering size and change when that size changes (F9), to support a baseline audio and video codec (F10), to keep streams and data safe from wiretapping (F11, F12) and to hide the host IP address from the other party (F14).

The next group covers the network and topology: reference frame insertion (F16), surviving a change of network interface (F17), working through NATs and firewalls that block UDP (F18), using several STUN and TURN servers (F19), using STUN and TURN servers supplied by the network rather than the application (F20), working through a proxy-only firewall (F21) and taking advantage of network quality-of-service capabilities to differentiate voice, video and data (F22). A third group covers multiple peers and streams (F23 to F26), a fourth covers audio processing such as spatialisation and voice activity levels (F27 to F30), a fifth covers legacy interoperation with telephony (F31 to F33) and the last covers unreliable datagram traffic, reliable data traffic and screen sharing (F34 to F36).

Appendix A lists the API requirements. The API must let the application ask the browser for permission to use cameras, microphones and the local file system (A1), control how streams are used and rendered (A2, A3), start and stop sending and receiving (A4, A9, A10), choose and later change the codec (A5, A6), be told whether a stream was set up successfully and whether a peer's stream has stopped or is being lost badly (A7, A11, A12), mute and unmute while keeping the mute status visible to the peer (A8), apply spatialisation, detect and adjust levels and mix audio (A13 to A16), identify streams so the same stream can be matched across peers (A17), send and receive isolated data chunks (A18), declare the type of audio signal (A19), state which media types it will accept (A20), ask for permission to share the screen (A21), name several STUN and TURN servers (A22), set a priority for outgoing streams and data (A23), send and receive files (A24), ask the browser to withhold the host IP address (A25) and read the statistics needed to estimate service quality (A26).
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements are numbered so they can be referred to precisely. F1 to F15 cover the basics of a call, F16 to F22 cover the network, F23 to F30 cover group calls and audio processing, F31 to F36 cover older telephone systems and other extras. Appendix A does the same for the programming interface the web application calls.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Section 4 splits the risks between the browser and the web application. A malicious web application might use the browser to mount a denial-of-service attack on NAT infrastructure or on peer devices. It might leak TURN credentials to unauthorised parties, letting them consume the TURN server's bandwidth; the answer is that web applications should be ready to revoke credentials and issue new ones. A malicious application might also silently establish outgoing streams and accept incoming streams on an already established connection.

On the browser side, the document expects mechanisms for obtaining user consent to use device resources such as the camera and microphone, for telling the user that those resources are in use, and for letting a user revise or completely revoke that consent. The same set of mechanisms is expected for the screen, a part of it, or the contents of a particular application window. The browser is also expected to let users verify that received streams have not been manipulated (F12), and it must ensure that media is neither sent nor rendered until the stream establishment and handshake procedures with the remote peer have finished successfully. Finally the browser must ensure that the stream negotiation procedures cannot be mistaken for a denial-of-service attack by other entities.

The web application is expected to make sure the user consents to sending and receiving media streams. Requirement F13 is the strongest statement in the document: the browser must encrypt, authenticate and integrity protect media and data on a per-IP-packet basis, and it must drop incoming media and data packets that fail the per-IP-packet integrity check. It must also support a mechanism for cryptographically binding media and data security keys to the user identity, referring to R-ID-BINDING in RFC 5479.
sections.plainLanguage: The security section says two things. The browser must ask permission before it uses the camera, the microphone or the screen, and it must not send or play any media until the handshake with the other side has finished. Every media packet must be encrypted and checked, and a packet that fails the check is thrown away rather than passed to the application.

items.title: F1 to F15
items.text: Common and basic: devices, NATs, rate control, rendering, echo cancellation, codecs, protection and statistics.

items.title: F16 to F22
items.text: Network and topology: reference frames, interface changes, UDP blocking, several STUN and TURN servers, proxy-only firewalls and quality of service.

items.title: F23 to F26
items.text: Multiple peers and streams: send to and receive from several peers, render several streams and mix several audio streams.

items.title: F27 to F30
items.text: Audio processing: spatialisation, measuring and changing the voice activity level, mixing other sound objects.

items.title: F31 to F33
items.text: Legacy interoperation: telephony codecs, navigating DTMF voice response systems, session setup carried in SIP.

items.title: F34 to F36
items.text: Other: short-latency unreliable datagram traffic, reliable data traffic and screen sharing.
